“Unless we put medical freedom into the Constitution, the time will come when medicine will organize into an undercover dictatorship to restrict the art of healing to one class of men and deny equal privileges to others: The Constitution of this Republic should make a special privilege for medical freedom as well as religious freedom.”
-- Dr. Benjamin Rush, signer of the Declaration of Independence

Posted September 9, 2002
Analysis By Richard Cowan

If someone accepts the recommendations of the Canadian Special Senate Committee on Illegal Drugs’s call for the legalization of cannabis, then one must necessarily conclude that cannabis prohibition has been more than just a mistake.

“Oops” is not a sufficient response. Clearly, this has been a major violation of human rights. Six hundred thousand Canadians , and over 14 million Americans , have been arrested, and many have been imprisoned, for cannabis crimes.

Hundreds of thousands more have been arrested in other democracies.

Moreover, it is impossible to calculate the death and suffering that has been caused by the suppression of the medical use of cannabis. It has certainly involved millions of people over the just the last few decades since it became clear that cannabis could alleviate the suffering caused by many different diseases, disabilities and medications.
See
The Murder of Peter McWilliams -- An Indictment, Not an Obituary by Richard Cowan

How is that cannabis prohibition remained in effect in Canada for three quarters of a century, even though it is undeniable that it was based on a racist book's reefer madness?
See
The Racist Origins Of Canada’s Marijuana Prohibition Reported In the National Post.
and
Head of 1971 Canadian Commission Recommending Decriminalization of Marijuana: " Stands By Report "

It must be recognized that cannabis prohibition is both a moral disaster as well as a major malfunction of our democratic institutions.

I have argued that the two groups most responsible for this fiasco are the media and law enforcement.
See
The Prohibitionist Police State Versus The People. Analysis By Richard Cowan
and links

However, in the era of official medicine, cannabis prohibition could not have survived this long if it had not corrupted the medical professions as well.
See
How Marijuana Prohibition Corrupts All Of Our Institutions
 Medicine, Law Enforcement, Journalism
And How That Corruption Sustains Prohibitionism

This is ironic in that in 1937, when the DEAland Congress held hearings on the first federal Marihuana Tax Act, the American Medical Association’s representative was the only person to oppose it and point that there was no evidence to support the claims made by Harry Anslinger.

One might accept that doctors may have been intimidated into silent acquiescence, however there can be no justification for abandoning the welfare of their patients, given that the Hippocratic oath says, “First, do no harm.”

Similarly, at the institutional level there can be no justification for abandoning the fundamentals of the scientific method.

Is this too extreme a characterization of the situation? I would maintain that this is the inescapable implication of accepting the conclusions of the Canadian Senate Committee.

In a moment, we will see that there is overwhelming evidence of the failure of both the humanitarian and scientific imperatives of modern medicine in dealing with cannabis itself.

However, first we must consider that for decades the medical profession and medical science have failed even to acknowledge the facts of cannabis prohibition. In the last few years a number of medical associations, notably those in the UK and Canada, have called for the decriminalization of cannabis, meaning an end to arresting users. However, the fact that it took them several decades and a vast number of arrests for them to say even this much leaves them looking considerably less than bold and heroic.

The point is that the workings of cannabis prohibition are not theoretical. It is the application of state violence against the users, growers, and sellers of cannabis, and their families.
See
New Zealanders Analysis of the Consequences of the Violence of Marijuana Prohibition. Bravo!

Doctors have to deal with the consequences of violence in their practice. The level of violence in DEAland is so great that it is a major public health problem, and it is recognized as such.

There are even categories of violence: the abuse of domestic partners; child abuse; elder abuse, etc. Moreover every doctor is familiar with the alcohol related violence that pours into emergency rooms on weekends.

There is even a medically recognized condition called post-traumatic stress syndrome.

Traumatic stress does not require that the victims have been physically injured. It may result from having been the victim of force via threats of violence or even just witnessing the application of force against others. Force, meaning either the use of or threat of force, is the essential ingredient in law enforcement, the state monopoly on violence.

These are not theories, but definitions, and it happens thousands of times a day to cannabis users in the Western democracies. But where is the recognition of this violence by the medical professions? Where are the studies of the consequences of being arrested?

Medical professionals are no longer just the silent victims of law enforcement. They are silent about it because they are complicit in it. They have become a part of it.

Official medicine not only decides whether or not the sick and dying can be prescribed a plant, it decides whether or not the citizens of ‘free countries’ can have the freedom to choose to use a plant based on its “professional” determination of the “safety” of the plant. However, if official medicine is truly concerned about the safety of the patients and the people at large, then how can it not be concerned about the violence of cannabis prohibition?

The violence of cannabis prohibition is thus a scientific fact of life and of death that is actually being promoted by the very profession that should be most opposed to it.

Arrogance and Ignorance

For the apogee of arrogance, consider this from a September 5th Ottawa Citizen article by Richard Starnes.

“A Carleton University professor who has been studying the effects of marijuana for more than 20 years is shocked by yesterday's call for the government to legalize the use of marijuana.

" We are not knowledgeable enough about the effects of marijuana to legalize it, " said Peter Fried.

Mr. Fried, who testified before the Senate Committee that made the recommendations, sounded astonished and admitted he finds the move hard to believe. He agrees with the conclusion that marijuana is not as harmful as either tobacco or alcohol but says that is no reason to legalize it.

" There is no doubt if we knew then what we know now about tobacco it would not have been legal, " he said. " I agree there is a lot of evidence that marijuana is more beneficial than other drugs for certain diseases. But if we had any other drug on the market about which there was so little known as marijuana, Health and Welfare Canada would not allow it. "

Mr. Fried, whose 22-year study following the offspring of parents who smoked marijuana during pregnancy is the longest of its kind in the world, says even now he does not know enough to confidently condone smoking for pregnant women.

" Should there be warning on packages? A woman who is nursing, should she smoke? And what about second-hand smoke or marijuana smoking in restaurants? Goodness gracious, there are so many questions. "

Goodness gracious, indeed.

" We are not knowledgeable enough about the effects of marijuana to legalize it. "???

This formulation is the very essence of the totalitarianism under which everything that is not specifically permitted is therefore prohibited.

In a free society our premise must rather be that if we don’t know enough about cannabis to legalize it, then we don’t know enough about cannabis to criminalize it.

The ultimate arrogance here is that doctors and medical researchers cannot --in their professional capacities -- be accepted as experts on whether or not cannabis or anything else should be legal or illegal.

In logic this fallacy is called ‘appeal to authority.’ Public policy in the use of criminal law is not medicine. Moreover, there is a division within the medical community about cannabis and cannabis prohibition. Unfortunately, this error is very common in the public discourse, but it is particularly offensive when people arrogate to themselves a mantle of authority that they are not entitled to wear.

Consider that if there was a debate on whether or not the water and sewer system should be publicly or privately owned, would it be logical to call on plumbers for their expert opinion?

Plumbers work everyday with the water and sewer system, just as doctors and researchers work with humans, but no one would make the same mistake that is made by asking doctors about the law -- or the police about psychopharmacology. In fact, the police per se are not even experts in public policies. They do not have degrees in any of the relevant disciplines, and there is also a difference of opinion within the ranks just as there is among doctors.

Nonetheless, we are told that we have to wait to change laws because they “are not knowledgeable enough about the effects of marijuana to legalize it.”

And the police are even claiming to be guardians of the public health, except for donuts.

Now The National Association of Professional Police, (NAPP) have joined the Canadian Police Association in opposing the legalization of cannabis.

However, the NAPP has added a new twist to the game. They have asked federal Health Minister Anne McLellan to take the lead in cabinet and view the possible legalization of pot as a serious health and social issue.

The full text of the NAPP press release is below. It has the usual prohibitionist objections, and “NAPP President Brian Adkin also points out that the use of marijuana, like the use of tobacco, poses a health risk to those who smoke it. Smoke of any kind, drawn into the lungs, will surely have adverse effects on long-term users. We do not need to add another burden to an already-strained health care system.

They are supported in their concern about smoking by doctors who misuse both their authority and science.

I have recently dealt with the problems created by organized medicine for Canadian medical cannabis patients.
See
Cruelty, Incompetence, And Quackery Threaten Canadian Medical Cannabis Patients.

Doctors “in their professional capacity “ have to decide whether or not a particular patient could benefit from a particular substance. However, the doctor/patient relationship is destroyed when the medical profession allies itself with the state monopoly on violence to prohibit a doctor and the patient from doing what they think is in the patient’s best interest.

Moreover, those doctors who seek to arrogate such authority for their profession rather look after the welfare of their own patients are apt to be intellectually dishonest as well.

Consider the example of Dr. Raju Hajela of Kingston, Ont. who is president of the Kingston-based Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine.

In the above link it was reported that the Canadian Health Minister's announcement that she was delaying making cannabis available to the sick and dying was made in response to a question from Hajela. It was actually applauded by the quacks.

Dr Hajela was quoted by The Globe and Mail as saying, " It's estimated that one marijuana joint is as harmful as about 10 cigarettes.”

There's no scientific evidence for the benefit. In my clinical practice, I see the harmful effects every day. "

The well-known science-fiction writer, Spider Robinson responded with a column in which he said described having “vomited nonstop for the next eight hours”.

This column's about what they did for my nausea that day -- which was nothing. They shot me up with four successive drugs, starting with Gravol ( a standard dose ) and working up to the mightiest antinausea drug in the pharmacopoeia, without effect. I retched continuously until it was simply not possible for my stomach to clench any more; then, thank God, I was able to persuade them to stop helping me, and let me go. My problem soon vanished.”
For the full text see
http://www.mapinc.org/drugnews/v02/n1636/a04.html?2057

Once again, the standard pharmaceutical anti-nausea drugs did not work. Their manufacturers do not claim that they always work. This is why some people need cannabis in this context. Also the pharmaceuticals are very expensive, so some people cannot afford them. In his column Robinson went on to call Hajela's claim that a single joint is as harmful as 10 cigarettes preposterous.

Hajela responded with a letter to the editor of The Globe and Mail: Where there's smoke
September 5, 2002, Page A20
“I read The Flin Flon Flip-Flop by Spider Robinson (Sept. 2) with interest, notwithstanding his potshots at the medical profession, Anne McLellan and me.

For those interested, marijuana smoke produces 50 per cent more tar and contains 70 per cent more benzopyrene than the same weight of tobacco. Marijuana smokers generally take a two-thirds larger puff volume, one-third greater depth of inhalation, and a fourfold longer breath-holding time than tobacco smokers. So it is easy to see how researchers arrive at the estimate of joint/cigarette harm of about 1:10 when one looks at acute and chronic respiratory symptoms of smoking, in addition to the risk of cancers.

Chemically, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) in marijuana is a hallucinogen that interferes with perception and is addictive.
See
No Evidence That THC Is Addictive Says Maker of Marinol
After 9 Month Study Including Law Enforcement

I have many patients who turned to marijuana for comfort but ended up with destruction of various aspects of their lives.

Marijuana has been around for millenniums, but it has not become popular as good medicine precisely because its safety and efficacy are not established. As a science-fiction writer, Mr. Robinson can invent ideas that sound scientific; but he must remember that science related to our daily lives needs to be grounded in reality.”

Raju Hajela MD, past president, Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine
See
The Real Data On Teen Marijuana " Abuse Treatment " What The Media Don't Tell Us: " Half of marijuana treatment admissions were referred through the criminal justice system. " -- Analysis By Richard Cowan

How odd. I would have thought that vomiting “nonstop for the next eight hours” is about as ‘grounded in reality’ as anything is likely to be.

Certainly, it is better grounded in reality than to oppose the medical use of cannabis because the way that recreational users of marijuana inhale illegal and therefore very expensive weed. Of course, he ignores vaporization, which would make the whole subject irrelevant, but his claims -- and those of his allies in the police -- about the dangers of cannabis to the respiratory system are not supported by the scientific evidence.

On May 14, 1997, the huge California HMO issued a press release saying, “In. an exhaustive study of ten years of mortality data for over 65,000 men and women, Kaiser Permanente research scientists found no statistically significant association between marijuana smoking and death.”

Similarly, in January of 1997 the National Drug And Alcohol Research Centre of Australia reported, “A study of 268 cannabis smokers who, on average, had smoked for 19 years and 31 non-using partners and family members, concluded that the health of the long-term smokers is virtually no different to that of the general population.”

In 1994, Dr. Donald Tashkin, a pulmonologist and UCLA professor of medicine, and a leading NIDA-funded researcher, concluded heavy marijuana use did not cause the same degree of lung injury as tobacco smoke.

" My own feeling is that marijuana smokers probably will not develop emphysema as a consequence of smoking marijuana, " he said, but cautioned that does not rule out the development of other conditions like respiratory carcinoma.

" It may be that the THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol) in marijuana could have different effects on inflammatory cells, which may mediate injury in the lung. "

In 1997, another study by Tashkin, et al, published in the American Journal of Respiratory Critical Care Medicine, Vol 155, No. 1, 01 1997, 141-148, said, “We conclude that regular tobacco, but not marijuana, smoking is associated with greater annual rates of decline in lung function than is nonsmoking. These findings do not support an association between regular marijuana smoking and chronic COPD but do not exclude the possibility of other adverse respiratory effects.”
Also see
Johns Hopkins Study Finds No Link Between Marijuana Use and Head, Neck, or Lung Cancer. There Was Also No Link Between This Study and Media Coverage.

Thus, we see a doctor using pseudo-science to justify the use of state violence against the sick and dying as well as the young and healthy under the pretext of saving them from the supposed dangers of cannabis that are not supported by the medical research.

We have another doctor saying we need to do more medical research before people can be free from the threat of state violence, because he does not yet know enough about the effect of cannabis.

However, we have no research being done about the effect of the very real violence being committed against the users of cannabis.

Whatever this may be, it is not science. It is not medicine. It is the corruption of the mind and soul of our society, and a major failure of our democratic institutions.

How appropriate in this context that the police would call upon the Health Minister to support the use of violence as a public health measure.

NAPP: Don't Legalize Pot
Don't Legalize Marijuana: National Association of Professional Police
Canada NewsWire
September 8, 2002
cnw@newswire.ca
http://www.newswire.ca

Canada's largest police associations oppose a Senate recommendation that the sale and use of marijuana be made legal.

The 24,000-member National Association of Professional Police, (NAPP) has asked federal Health Minister Anne McLellan to take the lead in cabinet and view the possible legalization of pot as a serious health and social issue.

NAPP President Brian Adkin says the greatest concern Canada's police have is the potential cost in human lives of marijuana legalization, a substance known to cause cognitive impairment.

" There are currently no widely-accepted and easily-administered tests available to detect whether someone's judgement or ability to function has been compromised by marijuana use, " says Adkin.

" For those who drink and drive, we have the breathalyser. But there is no way for us to know whether the driver next to you on the road or the pilot flying a plane or someone operating heavy machinery is under the influence of marijuana. There is no way for us to know whether they pose a danger to lives of others, " he adds.
See
UK Study on Marijuana and Driving Again Shows That It Is Not A Significant Factor in Accidents. Should We Arrest People for Being Tired?
and links, including
Canadian Study Confirms That Marijuana Impairs Driving Far Less Than Alcohol

Adkin also points out that the use the use of marijuana, like the use of tobacco, poses a health risk to those who smoke it. " Smoke of any kind, drawn into the lungs, will surely have adverse effects on long-term users. We do not need to add another burden to an already-strained health care system ".

In asking the federal Health minister to oppose the legalization of pot, NAPP points out that the many serious ramifications of marijuana legalization have not been adequately studied, particularly the effects that legalization would have on the competitiveness and quality of our schools, colleges and universities with students as young as 16 being permitted to smoke marijuana.

" We urge that no move toward decriminalization nor legalization of marijuana be made without exhaustive public consultation nor without expert advice from those involved in the fields of justice, law enforcement and medicine, " the Association concludes.
